docs.text: There will be hurricanes in Toronto this year. The Great Lakes will have multiple hurricanes.

To use more precise language, this post should read: “There is a high probability that surface temperatures of the Great Lakes will be high enough this year to cause tropical cyclone-like storms (hurricanes). There may even be multiple such storms. The last such hurricane was in 1996 in Lake Huron”

Hurricanes form using the energy in large bodies of water. Heat is energy. The more heat is in a body of water the more energy there is for a hurricane to form. If 80% of the Great Lakes usually are frozen in February but now it’s 0% then by July what do you think will be the temperature? Warm?
The last time there was a hurricane in the Great Lakes was in 1996 with the hurricane in Lake Huron:

An interesting article from 2020 looking back at the time a hurricane formed over the Great Lakes in 1996. One of the key ingredients was very high surface temperatures in the Great Lakes combined with a low pressure system and other factors in the weather patterns of that day.
A look back at "Hurricane Huron" over Lake Huron on 14 September 1996, viewed using Visible images from .bsky.social #GOES8/#GOESEast: cimss.ssec.wisc.edu/satellite-bl...
I think it's nice that the Great Lakes are capable of generating their own hurricanes. Or "huroncanes" en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_La...
They’re gonna do Great Lakes hurricanes by 2050
In 1996 a hurricane formed over Lake Huron.
I wonder, as Lake Michigan keeps warming, if we'll start having hurricanes in Michigan.

Somehow, I'm watching a video about hurricanes that form in places where they don't belong. Like Lake Erie, the southern coast of Brazil, or out in the Med over Greece. Even the one that hit Tijuana 2 years ago made the list. It cause sink holes everywhere. Folks lost homes.

Yes, it is. FEMA isn’t going to be around for tornadoes, hurricanes and floods. And, who gets hit the most by violent storms, the red states. Hurricanes don’t form on the Great Lakes or Norther Atlantic. All I can say is make certain your home is well insured.

I have been watching the systems come across America, ones with circulation seem to gain momentum when they hit the Great Lakes. This could become a point where hurricanes form here and move east towards England. If one actually meets up with another system, it could increase the size dramatically.
You can do it on any of the great lakes and not worry about hurricanes 😅
if the great lakes got warm enough, could they spawn hurricane-like storms?

Indeed. I’d say we will more likely see Mediterranean-style hurricanes like we saw the last few months starting to develop over the Great Lakes - whenever the temperature exceeds around 26 Celsius over a period of at least a few weeks. And they’re likely to ravage areas around the lakes.
(And yes one of the Great Lakes did have a hurricane a couple of decades ago, and the Mediterranean had an unexpectedly bad hurricane in 2023 which hit Libya and Greece)

I am skeptical you will ever see true hurricane formation over as small an area as the <100k sq miles of the Great Lakes, especially since each lake is largely separated from the other lakes by land, even if surface temps start to top 26 C...1/2

Hurricanes develop over warm seas & lose their power as they come inland. We have the Great Lakes to provide fuel for this storm. The water is relatively warm compared to the air. Water in general retains more heat than land. The Lakes are so big, they're like small oceans. 7/16

Actually it doesn't. The great lakes are already above sea level and are thus unaffected by sea level rise, and they do not get hurricanes.
In September 1996, a category 1 hurricane developed over Lake Huron. The first tropical storm ever recorded developing independently over the Great Lakes. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_La...
TIL about Hurricane Huron, a cyclone that formed over the Great Lakes in September 1996 and peaked at 992mb with 75 mph winds. en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_La...

(Yes, the Great Lakes have previously produced a hurricane, perhaps not *technically* a hurricane but it certainly was hurricane force similar to Mediterranean hurricane Daniel which hit Greece and Libya this year)
